AI NOTE — Caption 5 of the elephant-path chart. 5a/ is a folio marker fused to the head syllable of glang po, and [5] is the editor's caption number; neither is text, so neither is linked, and the first span begins at glang, not at the start of the string.One Tibetan verb, two English verbs. The wylie is a single clause on the pattern A B dang, C D mtshon — one final verb governing both pairs (elephant→mind, black color→dullness). The English needs a verb in each half, so Geshe Michael renders that one mtshon twice: represents in the first clause, symbolizes in the second. Only one can own the link, and it goes to symbolizes, the finite verb standing where mtshon actually stands. represents is the distributed second realization of the same verb and stays unwrapped — correct and expected, not an omission. The neighbouring caption confirms the pattern rather than the word choice: segment 172 has the identical frame (sprel 'phro ba dang , kha dog nag pa rgod pa mtshon) and renders it "The monkey stands for distraction, and his black color represents agitation." Tibetan kha dog nag pa is head-then-modifier ("color, black"), English is modifier-then-head ("black color"); Tibetan puts the object before the verb (bying ba mtshon) where English puts it after ("symbolizes dullness"). Both invert. Each is quarantined under a d=5 parent that spans the whole phrase against the whole English phrase — exactly licensed, nothing extra — with the members riding at d=7 inside it. The d=5 layer therefore runs forward in both languages, and the inversion never reaches the top row. This is why mtshon and bying ba are not two flat d=5 spans: listed flat they would cross the cursor.Not linked, deliberately. your in "your mind" and his in "his black color" have no Tibetan licensor — there is no genitive or possessive anywhere in the wylie, only bare sems and kha dog; these are the English supplying the second-person address the chart implies. So sems takes "mind", not "your mind", and the noun phrase takes "black color", not "his black color". The is an article belonging to nobody. The comma and shad are punctuation. po is carried as a null d=7 member of glang po. The nominalizer ba inside bying ba is real but is not listed: bying ba is itself a d=7 member here, and there is no depth below 7 to hang it from — "dullness" already carries it in the -ness counted on its parent.Cross-references. glang po for the mind is not new here: it comes from the Bhavaviveka verse quoted at segment 156, "Master the elephant of the mind" (yid kyi glang po), which the chart illustrates. The caption's bying ba / rgod pa pair, however, is not drawn from the nine-state list — segments 157–159 name the nine mental states, the six powers and the four modes of focus, and dullness and agitation appear in none of them. Their prose treatment comes later: 204 (both abundant in states one and two), 207 (subtle dullness in state five), 208–209, and 190. The rendering of bying ba as "dullness" is stable across all of them, and the black itself is resolved at 191, where glang po'i nag cha zad — "the elephant has lost all the black."
C03/c3p58: AI NOTE — Caption 6 of the elephant-path chart (the nine states of shamatha). Structure: two clauses sharing one clause-final verb — "sprel 'phro ba dang , kha dog nag pa rgod pa mtshon" = "[the] monkey — distraction, and [its] black color — agitation, [these it] represents." Geshe Michael renders the one Tibetan verb as two finite English verbs, "stands for" and "represents". Only one can be licensed by mtshon, so mtshon is linked to "represents", which sits in mtshon's own clause and in the same final position. "stands for" is deliberately left UNWRAPPED — the first clause has no overt Tibetan verb of its own, and double-linking one Tibetan word to two English verbs would manufacture evidence. DIRECT PARALLEL, segment 171: "5a/glang po sems dang , kha dog nag pa bying ba mtshon" = "[5] The elephant represents your mind, and his black color symbolizes dullness." Identical frame, identical kha dog nag pa, identical single final mtshon — but the English distributes the two verbs the other way round (171 puts "represents" in the FIRST clause and "symbolizes" in the second; 172 puts "stands for" first and "represents" second). Anyone aligning 171 should therefore expect mtshon to bind to a different slot than it does here; the two captions are not parallel in their English even though they are parallel in Tibetan. 171/172 are a matched pair: elephant + black = mind + dullness; monkey + black = distraction + agitation. Segments 157-159 name the nine mental states and the six powers and four modes of focus, but rgod pa and bying ba appear nowhere in 155-162. The agitation/dullness pair enters the course only with this caption series (171, 172, then 177, 180, 184, 191) and only later returns to prose at 204-212. So the caption is introducing terms, not echoing them. TERM NOTES. rgod pa = "agitation" is stable across the course (177 rgod pa'i yul "the various objects that agitation focuses upon"; 184; 208; 191). "distraction", however, is shared by two different Tibetan words: 'phro ba here and at 185 (sems ... la 'phro ba, rendered verbally as "distracted"), against g-yeng ba at 163 ("give up all distraction") and 181 ("your mind is wandering"). A reverse lookup on "distraction" will pull both; they are not interchangeable — 'phro ba is the mind spilling outward onto another object, g-yeng ba the mind straying. WYLIE ODDITY. The monkey is spelled sprel here; at 191 the same animal in the same chart is spre'u ("left behind the monkey as well"). Both are attested for "monkey" but a string search on either spelling alone will miss half the chart. BOUNDARY DECISIONS. kha dog nag pa is kept as ONE d=5 span rather than split into kha dog = "color" and nag pa = "black": the members would cross, since English puts "black" before "color", which would place a child out of order inside its own phrase. The compound maps onto "black color" exactly, with nothing left over. Unwrapped English, all correct: "[6]" (caption number, matching the folio marker's apparatus status), "The", "stands", "for" (part of the unlinked English phrasal verb, not any Tibetan particle), "and" (see s5), and "his" — there is no genitive or possessive anywhere in the wylie, kha dog nag pa is bare, so "his" has no Tibetan licensor and must not be absorbed into the "black color" span. The shad and comma between dang and kha dog are punctuation and are not linked.

AI NOTE — Caption [7] of the numbered legend to the elephant-path (shamatha) chart described at §156-§166. Not linked as apparatus: the wylie's "7a/" and the English's "[7]". Wylie oddity worth recording: these markers are not folio sides — §176 has "1a0/" for [10] and §178 "1a2/" for [12], so the "a" is a slot filler sitting between digits. The marker simply restates the caption number. THE SUBSTANTIVE CORRECTION TO BOTH PROPOSALS. A and B independently agreed that "to bring your mind back to the object" is an unlicensed expansion — B called it "Geshe Michael's gloss of what the effort is for." It is not. In this very caption series, §168 renders the bare wylie "dran pa" as "Bringing the mind back to the object", §169 renders "shes bzhin" as "Watchfulness", and §158 gives "dran pa'i stobs" as "the power of bringing your mind back to the object" against "shes bzhin gyi stobs" as "the power of watchfulness". dran shes here is the standing abbreviation of that pair, and the English distributes it: "...effort needed to bring your mind back to the object, and the degree of watchfulness needed." So dran and shes each have a real exponent and are linked at d=7 (s25, s26), and the parent dran shes is null — a contiguous English span covering both members would have to swallow ", and the degree of", which is exactly the over-capture the audits flag. Both proposals' dran shes = "watchfulness" gave the whole compound only its second member's English. Term check against the prose, since the caption is meant to gloss it. sems gnas bdun pa matches §157-§158 word for word (same sems gnas + ordinal frame; §158 uses bdun pa for the seventh). But the caption's word for effort is 'bad rtsol, whereas §158 assigns the seventh and eighth states to brtson 'grus kyi stobs, "the power of effort". These are different Tibetan words sharing one English word, and they are not making the same claim: §158's brtson 'grus is the power that produces states 7-8, while the caption's 'bad rtsol is the exertion of mindfulness-and-watchfulness whose magnitude the flames depict from state 1 up to state 7. A translator should not merge them, and a concordance on "effort" will pull both.
